prompt:
You are helping me generate a shortlist of brand-name candidates for a new company using {{vendor}}, our configured AI assistant. Before starting, ask me for any of the following that you don't already have: (1) a one- or two-sentence description of what the company does, (2) the industry or category, (3) target audience/customer, (4) any keywords, themes, or values I want reflected in the name, (5) tone/style preference (e.g., playful, technical, classic, invented word), (6) how many candidates I want (default to 20 if I don't specify), and (7) any names, words, or spellings to avoid.

Once you have these inputs, use {{vendor}}'s document creation and editing capabilities to produce a working document (exportable file) containing the candidate list. For each candidate name, include: the name itself, a one-line rationale tying it to my inputs, and a rough category tag (e.g., descriptive, invented, compound, metaphorical). Aim for a mix of styles unless I specify otherwise. Use {{vendor}}'s AI-generated insights to surface non-obvious but relevant word associations, wordplay, or naming patterns from my description and keywords.

Iterate with me: after the first draft, ask if I want more of a particular style, fewer of another, or different tone adjustments, and revise the document accordingly using {{vendor}}'s editing feature until I confirm the list is ready.

Do not check domain availability, social handles, or trademark conflicts in this step — that happens later. Your job here is only to generate and refine the candidate list.

When done, report back with: the total number of candidates produced, a summary of the naming styles/themes covered, and the exported document (or its location) containing the full list for my review.

You are helping me evaluate brand-name candidates for my new company. Please ask me for: (1) the list of candidate names I want checked, (2) my preferred domain extensions (e.g., .com, .io, .co), (3) the social platforms I care about (e.g., Instagram, X/Twitter, TikTok, LinkedIn, YouTube), and (4) the country/jurisdiction whose trademark register matters most to me (e.g., USPTO for the US, EUIPO for the EU).

For each candidate name, do the following:
1. Domain availability: check the exact name plus close variants across my requested extensions using a WHOIS lookup or a domain registrar's availability search (e.g., via Namecheap or GoDaddy's public search page). Note which extensions are free vs. taken.
2. Social handle availability: visit each requested platform and check whether the exact handle (and one or two close variants) is available or already claimed. Note follower count/activity if the handle is taken, so I can gauge conflict severity.
3. Trademark conflicts: search the relevant trademark office's public database (e.g., USPTO TESS for the US, or the EUIPO database for the EU) for exact and close matches in relevant business categories. Also run a general web search for existing companies using the name to catch unregistered but active conflicts.

Compile a single table with columns: Name | Domain status (per extension) | Social handle status (per platform) | Trademark/usage conflict findings | Overall risk score (low/medium/high) with a one-line rationale.

Done looks like: every candidate has been checked across all three dimensions with sources noted, and the table is complete with an overall risk score for ranking. Report back the full table plus a short summary recommending the top 2-3 names with the fewest conflicts.

You are helping me finalize the branding step for my startup by presenting a ranked list of candidate company names. Use {{vendor}} (my configured AI assistant) to do this.

First, ask me for: (1) the list of brand-name candidates already generated along with their scores/notes on domain availability, social handle availability, and trademark conflict risk — if I haven't provided this, ask me to paste it or point you to the file/document where it lives; (2) any weighting preference I have (e.g., domain availability matters more than social handles) — if I have none, use an even weighting across the three criteria; (3) how many top candidates I want shortlisted (default to 5 if I don't specify).

Once you have the inputs, use {{vendor}}'s document and code capabilities to: compute a composite score per candidate from the three criteria, rank all candidates from highest to lowest score, and produce a clean, exportable table (in a document or spreadsheet format) showing name, domain status, social handle status, trademark risk level, composite score, and rank. Where any scoring inputs look stale or incomplete, use {{vendor}}'s web-grounded search to double-check current domain/social/trademark status and cite the sources you used to confirm or update any entries.

Done looks like: a ranked, exportable document listing all candidates with their individual scores, composite score, and a short rationale note for the top-ranked options, plus citations for any freshly verified data.

Report back with: the finalized ranked list (top candidates highlighted), the file/document you produced and its location or export format, and any candidates where data was uncertain or conflicting so I can review them myself.

You are helping me generate AI-created logo images for my brand. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) my brand name, (2) a short description of my brand's tone/industry (e.g., playful fintech, minimalist wellness), (3) any preferred colors, styles, or symbols, and (4) how many logo concepts I want (default to 4-6 if I don't specify).

Using OpenAI's image generation API (DALL-E) with my configured credentials, generate the requested number of distinct logo concepts based on the brand details I provide. Write clear prompts that specify: the brand name (if it should appear as text in the logo), a clean vector/flat-icon style suitable for a logo, transparent or white background, and the tone/colors I specified. Generate a few style variations (e.g., wordmark, icon-only, combination mark) if I haven't specified a single style.

Save each generated image locally or to my configured storage with a clear filename convention (e.g., brandname_logo_01.png, brandname_logo_02.png, etc.) so they can be reviewed and compared later.

Done looks like: a set of generated logo image files saved and accessible, covering the number of concepts and style variations requested, each reasonably matching the brand description I gave.

Report back to me with: the list of saved filenames/paths, a brief description of what each logo depicts (style, colors, layout), and any notes on prompts that produced weaker results so I can decide whether to regenerate before moving to the next step (storing and setting a primary logo).

You are helping me finish branding step brand_002:n2 — set the primary logo among the AI-generated logo images we already created and stored. Before acting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear: (1) the brand name/project this logo belongs to, (2) where the generated logo image files currently live (e.g., a specific folder path, cloud storage bucket, CMS media library, or database table), (3) how many candidate logos exist and any naming/versioning convention already in use, and (4) any selection criteria I want applied (e.g., preferred style, color, file format, or a specific filename I already like).

Once you have this, do the following: list the available logo candidates from the location I gave you, confirm which one I want as primary (if I haven't picked one, present the options with brief descriptions and ask me to choose — do not choose for me), then mark that file as the primary logo using whatever mechanism the storage system supports — this could mean renaming/copying it to a canonical filename (e.g., 'logo-primary.png'), setting a metadata flag or database field, or updating a manifest/config file that other tools reference. Make sure any other systems that reference 'the logo' (site header config, brand style guide doc, README) point to this same file if you have access to update them.

When done, report back: which logo file was set as primary, the exact location/identifier now marking it as primary, and any files or references you updated. If you could not determine where to write the 'primary' designation, tell me exactly what information you still need.

You are helping me generate color palette directions for my brand based on a set of brand adjectives (the descriptive words that define our brand personality, e.g., 'bold, trustworthy, modern' or 'warm, playful, approachable'). 

First, ask me for: (1) my brand adjectives (3-5 words), (2) my company/domain name, and (3) any existing brand constraints (e.g., a color we must include, an industry norm to avoid, accessibility requirements like WCAG contrast compliance).

Once I provide these, do the following:
1. Translate each adjective into color psychology associations (e.g., 'trustworthy' often maps to blues, 'playful' to bright/warm hues).
2. Propose 3 distinct palette directions, each with a clear name/theme (e.g., 'Confident Blue', 'Warm Optimism', 'Modern Minimal'). For each direction, specify: a primary color, one or two secondary/accent colors, and a neutral (background/text) color, each with hex codes.
3. For each palette, briefly explain how it reflects the given adjectives and note its likely emotional tone.
4. Flag any accessibility concerns (e.g., low contrast between text and background) for each palette.
5. Present the three directions in a clear side-by-side summary (table or bulleted comparison) so I can easily evaluate trade-offs.

Done looks like: three well-differentiated, named palette directions, each with hex codes for primary/secondary/neutral colors, a rationale tying back to my adjectives, and accessibility notes — ready for me to review and pick one (or request adjustments) in the next step.

Report back with the full comparison and your recommendation for which direction best fits the stated adjectives, along with reasoning. Do not finalize or lock in a palette — this is a proposal step only.

You are helping me choose a direction for our brand color palette. This is a subjective creative decision, so your job is to prepare well-researched options for me to review and decide on — not to make the final choice yourself.

First, ask me for any details you need if I haven't already given them: our company/domain name, a short description of what we do, our target audience, our industry, any competitor brands to differentiate from or align with, and any existing brand assets (logo, colors already in use) I should account for.

Then do the following:
1. Research color psychology and palette conventions relevant to our industry and audience.
2. Use a tool like Coolors (or similar palette generator) or your own design knowledge to generate 4-6 distinct palette directions (e.g., "bold and energetic," "minimal and trustworthy," "warm and organic," etc.), each with a short name and 1-2 sentence rationale tying it to our brand and audience.
3. For each direction, list the actual hex codes for a primary color, a secondary color, an accent color, and a neutral/background color.
4. Briefly note any competitor or industry conventions each direction aligns with or deliberately breaks from.
5. Compile all of this into a single clear document or message, organized so I can quickly compare directions side by side.

Done looks like: I have a concise, well-organized set of 4-6 palette direction options with hex codes, rationale, and industry context, ready for me to review.

Report back with the full list of palette directions and their details, then stop for human sign-off — do not select a final direction, apply any colors to brand assets, or make the choice on my behalf. Wait for me to tell you which direction I want to move forward with.

You are helping me finalize the brand color palette for my organization by checking WCAG contrast and accessibility compliance before it's locked in.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already provided:
- My domain or brand name
- The current candidate color palette (hex codes for primary, secondary, accent, background, and text colors)
- Any existing style guide, logo, or brand asset references
- Whether I have specific use cases to check (e.g., button text on brand background, links on white, dark-mode variants)

Once you have the palette, do the following:
1. Compute contrast ratios for all realistic foreground/background pairings likely to appear in the product or marketing site (e.g., body text on background, button label on button fill, link color on background, white text on dark brand color).
2. Evaluate each pairing against WCAG 2.1 standards: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+/14pt bold+) and UI components; note where AAA (7:1) is also met.
3. Flag every pairing that fails AA, and for each failing pair propose one or two adjusted hex values (slightly darker/lighter shades of the same brand color) that would pass while staying visually close to the original intent.
4. Check the palette for color-blind safety (e.g., avoid relying on red/green alone to convey meaning) and note any concerns.
5. Produce a clear table: color pair, hex codes, contrast ratio, pass/fail for AA and AAA, and recommended fix if failing.

Done looks like: a complete contrast audit table covering all key pairings, with pass/fail status and concrete hex-code remediation suggestions for any failures, plus a short summary of overall accessibility risk.

Report back with the full table, the summary, and a final list of the recommended (possibly adjusted) palette hex codes ready for my review. Do not change official brand assets or publish anything — just prepare this analysis, since finalizing the palette remains a human step.

You are helping me set our finalized brand color palette as design tokens (variables) inside {{vendor}}, our design tool. 

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the final list of brand colors with names and hex values (e.g. Primary, Secondary, Accent, Neutral shades, Success/Error/Warning if defined), (2) the {{vendor}} workspace/team or project where these tokens should live, and (3) whether we need multiple modes/themes (e.g. Light and Dark) or just one default mode.

Once you have this, using your configured credentials and {{vendor}}'s API or plugin/token-management interface:
1. Create or open the relevant design file/library in {{vendor}}.
2. Create a color variable/token collection for our brand palette if one doesn't already exist.
3. Add each brand color as a named token with the correct hex value, matching the names I gave you.
4. If multiple modes were requested, set up those modes and assign correct values per mode.
5. Verify the tokens are saved and visible in the tool's variables/tokens panel, and that names and values exactly match what I provided.
6. If the API/plugin surface requires publishing or enabling library sharing for the tokens to be usable across files, complete that action as it is a routine configuration step, not a sign-off decision.

When done, report back: the name of the token collection/library, the full list of tokens created with their names, hex values, and mode assignments (if any), and a link or path to where they live in {{vendor}}. If any color name was ambiguous or you had to make a judgment call on naming/structure, flag it clearly in your report so I can review. Do not invent colors or modes I have not provided — ask me if anything is missing.

You are helping me begin our SOC 2 Type I compliance journey by preparing the account creation for {{vendor}}, our chosen compliance-automation platform. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: our company legal name, primary domain, the corporate email address or SSO provider we want to use for signup, the name/title of the authorized representative who will complete registration, and any organizational details (company size, industry) {{vendor}} typically requests during onboarding.
2. Research {{vendor}}'s signup flow (via their public website) and identify the exact fields required: account/org name, admin email, password or SSO method, billing/plan selection, and terms-of-service acceptance step.
3. Pre-fill a draft of the signup form with the information I provide, noting clearly which fields still need my input (e.g., payment card details, SSO credential entry) — describe these as form fields, not API calls, since no vendor API endpoints are in scope here.
4. Prepare a short checklist summarizing: (a) what account tier/plan looks appropriate for a SOC 2 Type I effort, (b) which Trust Services Criteria and policy templates we'll likely need to enable once inside the platform, and (c) what evidence-collection integrations (cloud provider, HR system, etc.) we should connect first after account creation.
5. Do NOT submit the signup form, accept {{vendor}}'s terms of service, enter payment/billing authorization, or log in with corporate SSO on my behalf — these require my direct action.

When finished, report back with: the pre-filled form draft, the checklist described above, and a clear list of the remaining fields/actions only I can complete. Then stop for human sign-off so I can review, enter credentials/payment, accept terms, and finalize the account myself.

You are helping me complete the 'Connect integrations' step of our SOC 2 Type I setup in {{vendor}}, our compliance automation platform. Please prepare (but do not finalize) the integration connections needed for evidence collection.

First, ask me for: (1) my {{vendor}} account login/workspace details, (2) the list of systems we need connected — typically our cloud provider(s), identity provider, code hosting, HR system, MDM, and ticketing tool, and (3) whether we have any custom/on-prem systems not in the standard catalog.

Then, using my configured credentials, log into {{vendor}} and navigate to its integrations catalog. For each standard system I name, locate the correct integration entry, confirm it uses read-only scopes where offered, and prepare it for connection — filling in any required configuration fields, but stop before triggering the OAuth authorization or credential-grant flow, since that requires my explicit consent per system.

For any custom or on-prem systems not in the catalog, check whether {{vendor}} supports custom connections via a documented API; if so, describe in words how a developer would create and list such connections so evidence can be pushed manually. Draft the specific setup steps for a developer to implement this, but do not execute API calls that grant access.

Produce a checklist listing: each system to connect, the scopes/permissions each integration will request, and which step requires my manual OAuth approval in the {{vendor}} UI. Flag any integration whose required permissions look broader than read-only so I can review them.

When your checklist and draft configurations are ready, present them to me and stop for human sign-off before any authorization is granted or integration is finalized.

You are helping me generate the initial set of security policies for our SOC 2 Type I journey using {{vendor}}, our compliance automation platform. If you don't already know them, ask me for: (1) our {{vendor}} account login/workspace details (confirm you can use your configured credentials to access it), (2) our company legal name and domain, and (3) the list of employees/roles who will need to accept policies.

Actions to take:
1. Log into {{vendor}} using your configured credentials.
2. Locate the policy template library and fetch the standard SOC 2 policy set (e.g., Information Security, Access Control, Data Classification, Incident Response, Change Management, Vendor Management, Business Continuity).
3. If {{vendor}} offers a built-in AI assistant, delegate drafting/customization of each policy to it, tailoring placeholders (company name, scope, roles, review cadence) to our details.
4. Set up or confirm version control and an approval workflow within {{vendor}} so each policy has a draft state, an editor history, and a designated approver.
5. Configure per-employee acceptance tracking so the platform will notify staff and log acknowledgments once policies are published.
6. Compile a summary checklist listing every policy generated, its current draft status, assigned approver, and any open placeholders needing my input.

Do not publish, finalize, or mark any policy as approved, and do not trigger employee acceptance notifications. This step requires that a human explicitly approve before changes are applied, so you must stop for human sign-off once drafts and the checklist are ready.

Report back with: the list of policies drafted, a link or path to each in {{vendor}}, the approval workflow status, any unresolved placeholders, and a clear note that you are stopping for human sign-off before publishing.

You are helping me prepare the SOC 2 Type I policy set inside Vanta ahead of human compliance review. Do not finalize, publish, or mark any policy as approved—your job is to draft and organize, not to approve.

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: my company domain, Vanta account access confirmation (assume I use my configured credentials), a description of our actual security practices (e.g., access control model, data handling, incident response process, vendor management, infrastructure/cloud setup), and any existing internal policy documents or wiki pages I want reflected.

Actions to take:
1. Log into Vanta and pull up the default policy templates it generated for our SOC 2 Type I program (e.g., Information Security Policy, Access Control Policy, Data Classification Policy, Incident Response Policy, Vendor Management Policy, etc.).
2. For each policy, compare the template language against the operational details I gave you and draft edits so the wording matches what we actually do (systems used, roles/titles, approval chains, review cadence).
3. Flag any policy sections where the template assumes a control we don't have in place, or where our practice is stricter/looser than the template implies—list these clearly as open questions rather than guessing.
4. Organize your output as a per-policy diff or summary: what Vanta's default said, what you propose changing, and why.

Done looks like: every relevant policy has a drafted redline and a list of unresolved judgment calls, all staged in Vanta as unpublished edits (not applied/approved).

Report back with the full list of policies reviewed, the proposed changes for each, and the open questions needing compliance/legal judgment. Then stop for human sign-off before any policy is approved or applied in Vanta.

You are helping me configure automated compliance tests in {{vendor}} as part of our SOC 2 Type I journey. Before doing anything, ask me for: (1) my {{vendor}} account access confirmation (assume you'll use my configured credentials), (2) which systems/integrations are already connected (cloud provider, identity provider, HR system, code repo, etc.), and (3) whether we're scoping to SOC 2 Type I Trust Services criteria only or adding any custom frameworks/controls.

Once you have that, use {{vendor}}'s test listing capability (the equivalent of the 'list tests' API) to pull the current set of automated tests mapped to our connected systems, and identify: which built-in tests are already active, which are failing or need a connection to run, and which controls have no test coverage yet. Where relevant, prepare a summary of any custom controls or custom tests we should add for our own internal policies, including proposed test logic and evidence source in words (no need to write code).

Compile a clear report grouped by: (a) tests already passing, (b) tests failing or blocked pending a system connection, (c) recommended custom tests/controls to add, and (d) any test configuration changes you'd propose (e.g., adjusting schedules, thresholds, or scope).

Do not enable, disable, or modify any test configuration yourself — only prepare the full list of recommended changes with rationale. Present this to me for review and then stop for human sign-off before any changes are applied in {{vendor}}.

You are helping me remediate failing compliance test results in our Vanta SOC 2 Type I monitoring dashboard. Please do the following:

1. If you don't already have it, ask me for access details or confirm you can use my configured credentials to log into Vanta.
2. Pull the current list of failing tests from the Vanta dashboard, grouped by integrated service (e.g., AWS, Google Workspace, GitHub, identity provider, HR system) and by control category (access control, encryption, logging, vulnerability management, etc.).
3. For each failing test, identify the root cause (e.g., MFA not enforced, unencrypted storage bucket, missing log retention policy, inactive user account not deprovisioned, missing vendor security review).
4. Draft a specific remediation plan per failing test: what setting needs to change, in which system, and the exact steps to change it. Where a fix requires a policy document update, draft the revised policy language.
5. Prioritize the list by risk severity and ease of fix, and flag any tests that require a business decision (e.g., choosing a new access policy) rather than a pure technical fix.
6. Compile everything into a single remediation report: test name, current status, root cause, proposed fix, system/owner affected, and estimated effort.

Do not make any configuration changes, update any policies, close out any tests, or mark anything remediated in Vanta yourself. Every change must be explicitly approved by a human before it is applied, since a human must explicitly approve before changes are applied. Prepare the full remediation plan and pre-filled drafts, then stop for human sign-off.

Report back with the complete failing-tests list, your remediation plan for each item, and a clear summary of which items are ready for one-click approval versus which need a policy decision from me first.

You are helping me operationalize the 'Employee security training' step of our SOC 2 Type I journey in Vanta. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for our Vanta account domain/login context if not already known, our employee roster (or the HR/people-ops source of truth, e.g. Google Workspace, BambooHR, or a spreadsheet I provide), and the deadline I want to set for training completion.
2. Using your configured credentials, log into Vanta and confirm the security training module is enabled and assigned to all current employees and contractors who need it (per our policy scope).
3. Cross-check the Vanta employee list against my roster to flag any missing, duplicate, or offboarded accounts, and prepare a list of discrepancies for me to resolve.
4. Draft a short reminder email/Slack message I can send to employees who haven't completed training yet, including the deadline and a link to the Vanta training portal.
5. Set up a recurring check (daily or every few days, your recommendation) where you poll Vanta's training completion dashboard and report back the current completion percentage, names of employees still pending, and any overdue past the deadline.
6. Note explicitly that actually completing each individual's training modules remains a human step — this is third-party-wait: each employee must log in and finish their own modules on their own schedule, and no agent action can complete that for them.

Done looks like: training assigned to all employees in Vanta, discrepancies list prepared, reminder draft ready, and a monitoring cadence established so I get regular completion-status updates until 100% is reached.

Report back with: current completion %, list of outstanding employees, any roster mismatches found, and the reminder draft text for my review.

You are helping me prepare to engage a SOC 2 Type I auditor as part of our Vanta compliance journey. This is a policy-gate step: you must prepare everything needed but cannot select a firm, negotiate terms, or sign any engagement letter — that requires an authorized officer's decision.

First, ask me for: (1) our company legal name and domain, (2) our target SOC 2 Type I audit window/deadline if known, (3) whether we have Vanta's list of pre-approved/integrated audit firm partners available, or whether I want you to compile a shortlist of reputable SOC 2 audit firms from public information, and (4) any budget range or firm-size preference (boutique vs. established).

Then do the following:
1. Research and compile a comparison list of 3-5 candidate SOC 2 audit firms (or use Vanta's partner directory if I provide access), including for each: firm name, relevant experience with SOC 2 Type I, typical turnaround time, and general pricing range if publicly available.
2. Draft an outreach email template requesting a proposal/engagement letter from shortlisted firms, referencing our company, desired report type (Type I), and target timeline.
3. Prepare a checklist of information the chosen auditor will likely need from us (system description scope, control list, policy documents, evidence collection status in Vanta).
4. Summarize the shortlist, draft outreach email, and checklist in a single document.

Done looks like: a ready-to-send comparison summary, outreach draft, and information checklist, all pending my review. Do not contact any firm, negotiate pricing, or sign or submit any engagement letter on my behalf — stop for human sign-off once materials are prepared. Report back with the shortlist, drafts, and a clear note that firm selection and contract signature remain my decision to make.

You are helping me monitor and prepare for the completion of our SOC 2 Type I audit, which we are running through Vanta with an independent third-party auditing firm. The actual conduct and sign-off of the audit examination remains a human step performed by the third-party auditor and cannot be completed or accelerated by you.

First, ask me for anything you need that you don't already have: our company domain, our Vanta account login status (confirm I can access it with my configured credentials), the name of the auditing firm we've engaged (if selected), and the expected audit start/end dates if known.

Then, using my configured credentials, log into our Vanta dashboard and:
1. Check the current audit status (e.g., evidence collection, auditor review, report drafting).
2. Compile a summary of any outstanding evidence requests, failed/at-risk controls, or unresolved policy gaps flagged in Vanta that could delay or block the auditor.
3. Identify any open auditor questions or requests visible in Vanta or via any auditor communication tools we use, and draft clear, factual responses I can review (do not send them yourself).
4. Note the last-updated timestamp on the audit status so we can track progress over time.

Do not sign, approve, submit, or communicate directly with the auditor on my behalf — only prepare drafts and summaries for my review.

Report back with: (a) current audit status and stage, (b) any outstanding items requiring my input or action, (c) drafted responses to auditor requests if any exist, and (d) a recommended date/time for you to poll Vanta again for status updates, since final completion depends on the auditor's independent testing timeline and remains a human step.

You are helping me prepare for the SOC 2 Type II observation window and scope negotiation with our audit firm. This negotiation itself remains a human step, since it requires back-and-forth professional judgment between me and the auditor's team based on their methodology and our risk profile — you cannot drive it.

What I need you to do instead is prepare all the materials so the actual conversation goes smoothly:

1. Ask me for: our company domain, the trust services criteria we're pursuing (e.g., Security, Availability, Confidentiality), the date our Type I report was issued, our current infrastructure/vendor stack, and the name of our audit firm if known.
2. Draft a one-page briefing document summarizing: our Type I scope and any exceptions noted, our proposed observation window (research typical ranges of 3, 6, or 12 months and note tradeoffs for enterprise buyer expectations), and any system/control changes since Type I that could affect scope.
3. Draft a list of clarifying questions to bring to the auditor, such as: what evidence cadence they expect, whether any new systems or subservice organizations should be added to scope, and how they handle control changes mid-window.
4. Prepare a checklist of internal readiness items (evidence collection tooling in place, control owners identified, calendar blocked for the window) so I can confirm we're ready to commit to a start date.

Once these materials are drafted, stop for human sign-off — do not contact the auditor, propose dates on my behalf, or finalize scope. Report back with the briefing document, the question list, and the readiness checklist, clearly labeled, and flag any gaps where you need more information from me before finishing the draft.

You are helping me configure continuous control monitoring in {{vendor}}, our compliance-automation platform, to begin the SOC 2 Type II observation window (our Type I setup is already complete in {{vendor}}).

First, ask me for: (1) my {{vendor}} account/org details if not already configured, (2) the list of systems in our real stack that need connecting — cloud provider(s), identity provider, HR system, code hosting, ticketing tool, and MDM — and (3) where I want alerts routed (Slack channel, email address, or ticketing queue).

Then, using {{vendor}}'s documented public API or integrations catalog:
1. Connect each system I specify with read-only scopes, using my configured credentials — do not request or handle raw keys/secrets beyond what {{vendor}}'s own connection flow requires.
2. Confirm each integration is active and pulling data on a schedule so evidence collection (timestamped, machine-gathered artifacts) replaces manual screenshots/CSV exports.
3. Verify that automated tests are enabled and running continuously against the Trust Services Criteria controls relevant to our Type II scope.
4. Configure alerting so control failures or configuration drift notify the destination I specified, with enough context (control ID, failing check, affected system) for remediation.
5. Review the built-in evidence requests and required policies for Type II and confirm they map to our connected systems and control set, flagging any gaps or unmapped controls.

Done looks like: every listed system connected and verified live, continuous testing confirmed running, alerting confirmed delivering to the right destination, and a clear list of any unmapped controls or missing integrations.

Report back with: a summary of connected systems and their scopes, confirmation continuous testing is active, the alert destination configured, and any gaps that need my attention before the observation window can be considered fully instrumented.

You are helping me track the SOC 2 Type II observation window, the 3–12 month period during which my controls must operate continuously before our auditor can begin fieldwork. The actual passage of time and the auditor's eventual attestation remains a human step you cannot accelerate or perform — please do not attempt to simulate or skip it.

What I need from you now is preparation and monitoring support. First, ask me for: (1) the start date of the observation window, (2) the planned end date (based on the window length I chose, e.g., 3, 6, or 12 months), (3) which compliance automation platform I use (if any) for continuous evidence collection, and (4) the auditor firm's name and contact if already engaged.

Once I provide these, please:
1. Create a simple tracking record (a checklist or timeline doc) showing the start date, end date, and key milestones (e.g., monthly control-evidence check-ins, mid-window review, pre-fieldwork prep deadline).
2. Draft a recurring reminder schedule (weekly or monthly) for me to verify that evidence collection is running without gaps — flag if my compliance platform shows any control test failures or missing evidence during this period.
3. Prepare a pre-fieldwork readiness checklist covering: management assertion draft, evidence completeness review, and auditor coordination steps, so I can act quickly once the window closes.

Once you have these, using {{vendor}}'s documented public API (e.g., an issue-creation mutation like IssueCreate), create one tracked issue per finding with: title summarizing the vulnerability, full description/repro details from the report, a severity label matching our mapping, the correct project/team, an assignee, and a due date derived from our SLA policy. If {{vendor}} supports custom fields or workflow statuses, set a 'Security Finding' or equivalent status/field so these are filterable separately from regular work. If {{vendor}} supports automation rules, set up (or confirm existing) rules so future findings of a given severity auto-route to the right assignee/queue, and if AI-based triage/prioritization is available, enable or verify it against our mapping.

Done looks like: every finding from the report has a corresponding tracked issue with severity label, assignee, and due date, all issues are queryable in one view/filter for our SOC 2 auditor and trust center evidence, and any automation rules are active for next year's cycle.

Report back: a list of created issue IDs/links mapped to original finding titles, the severity breakdown, and confirmation of any automation rules configured.

You are helping me remediate the critical and high findings from this year's penetration test before we can request the retest from the pen test firm. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) the pen test findings report or list of findings (file, PDF, or exported CSV), (b) the name of the issue tracker we use (e.g. Jira, Linear, GitHub Issues, Asana) and confirmation you have configured access to it, and (c) the name of our trust center or SOC 2 evidence folder if findings need to be logged there too.

2. From the findings report, extract every finding rated Critical or High. For each, capture: title, severity, affected asset/system, description, and the firm's recommended remediation.

3. Create or update a ticket in our issue tracker for each critical/high finding, using consistent naming (e.g. "PenTest-2025: [severity] [short title]"), tagging it appropriately (security, pentest, compliance) and setting priority based on severity.

4. Where the fix is a configuration or code change I can identify a clear owner for, draft the remediation plan or pull request description with the specific change needed (e.g. patch version, config setting, access control fix) based on the report's recommendation — but do not merge or deploy changes yourself unless I've explicitly told you that you have deployment authority for this environment.

5. Track status of each ticket until it is marked resolved, and compile a remediation summary listing: finding, severity, status (fixed/in progress/blocked), owner, and date closed.

Done looks like: every critical and high finding has a corresponding tracked ticket, a documented remediation action, and a status. Report back to me with the full list of findings, their current status, and the remediation summary, so I can confirm we're ready to request the retest letter.

You are helping me close out our annual penetration test by requesting the retest and formal attestation letter from the firm that performed the test. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the pen-test firm's name and how we communicate with them (client portal login details I'll provide access to, or the contact email/support form), (2) the list or tracker link of findings we've remediated (especially all criticals/highs), and (3) where our trust center or compliance repository lives so you know where the letter needs to end up.

Once you have this, do the following: draft a clear, professional retest request message referencing our engagement/project ID (ask me if unknown), listing each remediated finding by ID/title and stating it is ready for verification, and asking them to (a) perform the retest and (b) issue the formal attestation/retest letter confirming remediation status for our SOC 2 auditors and customers. Include a requested turnaround date if I give you one.

Send this via the vendor's client portal or their email/support form using your configured credentials or my logged-in session. After sending, monitor for their response and the delivered retest results and attestation letter. When the letter arrives, save it and update our findings tracker to mark each retested item as verified-closed, noting the retest date and letter reference.

Report back with: the date the request was sent, the channel used, the firm's response/status, and confirmation once the attestation letter is received and filed, including where it's stored for trust center use.

You are helping me triage an incoming security questionnaire before I decide how to prioritize and staff answering it. 

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already provided: the questionnaire file (spreadsheet or document) or its location, the deal/opportunity name, the deal size (ACV or TCV), the customer's stated deadline, and any CRM or deal-tracking system link where you can pull deal size/stage details using my configured credentials.

Then do the following:
1. Open the questionnaire and count total rows/questions, and identify its format (spreadsheet, form, portal export).
2. Scan the questions and tag each one by category (e.g., access control, data handling, encryption, incident response, subprocessors, compliance certifications) and flag any that look unusually invasive, non-standard, or high-risk (e.g., requests for source code, penetration test reports, subprocessor lists, or legal commitments).
3. Note the stated deadline and calculate business days remaining from today.
4. Pull the deal size and stage from the CRM or from what I tell you.
5. Summarize how many rows fall into each risk/category bucket, and estimate rough effort (e.g., number of questions likely answerable from existing knowledge-base content vs. ones needing new research or legal/security sign-off).

Produce a concise triage brief containing: deal name, deal size, deadline and days remaining, total question count, category breakdown, flagged high-risk questions, and an estimated effort split. Do not decide the priority tier or resourcing yourself — that judgment call belongs to me as the deal/security owner.

When the brief is ready, present it to me clearly and stop for human sign-off so I can decide how to prioritize this questionnaire against other deals and assign resourcing.

You are helping me prepare answers for an incoming security questionnaire (300-row spreadsheet) by pulling prior answers and policies from our {{vendor}} compliance-automation knowledge base. If you don't already have it, ask me for: (1) our {{vendor}} account/workspace URL, (2) the format and file of the incoming questionnaire (SIG, CAIQ, spreadsheet export, or portal name), and (3) which product/business unit this deal covers if we have multiple.

Using your configured credentials, log into {{vendor}} and:
1. Import the questionnaire in its native format (spreadsheet, SIG, CAIQ, or portal export) into {{vendor}}'s import tool so rows are structured for matching.
2. Run {{vendor}}'s knowledge-base search/match against our prior answered questionnaires and our current policy library (data retention, access control, incident response, encryption, subprocessors, etc.), pulling the most recent approved version of each relevant answer and policy.
3. For each row, attach the matched prior answer or policy excerpt as a suggested source, flagging rows with no match, conflicting matches, or matches to an outdated/superseded policy version.
4. Note any policies that are missing, expired, or unapproved per {{vendor}}'s versioning/approval tracking, so they can be flagged for review later in the process.
5. Compile a coverage summary: total rows, rows with a confident match, rows with partial/conflicting matches, and rows with no match at all.

Done looks like: every row in the questionnaire has either a linked prior answer/policy source or an explicit "no match" flag, and you have a coverage summary ready to hand off to the drafting step. Do not submit, finalize, or send anything to the customer — this step only assembles source material.

Report back with: the coverage summary numbers, a short list of flagged rows needing missing/outdated policies, and confirmation that the matched sources are staged in {{vendor}} for the next drafting step.

You are helping me draft answers to an enterprise security questionnaire using our existing policy corpus. Before starting, ask me for: (1) the location/export of the questionnaire spreadsheet (all ~300 rows), (2) access to our knowledge base of prior questionnaire answers, security policies, SOC2/ISO docs, and compliance artifacts, and (3) any specific customer name or portal context that might affect tone or required detail.

Once you have these, do the following:
1. Read through the questionnaire row by row, grouping questions by topic (e.g., access control, encryption, incident response, data retention, vendor management).
2. For each row, search the policy corpus and prior answers for the most relevant, up-to-date source language. Draft an answer using that source material, staying factually grounded — do not invent capabilities, certifications, or controls we don't have evidence for.
3. If no matching policy or prior answer exists for a question, mark the row clearly as "NO SOURCE FOUND — needs input" rather than guessing.
4. Flag rows that involve legal commitments, liability language, novel scope, or anything materially different from prior answers as "needs security review."
5. Add a short citation note per answer (which policy doc or prior questionnaire it was pulled from) so reviewers can verify quickly.

When done, produce an updated spreadsheet or document with: drafted answers, source citations, and a status column (Drafted / Needs Source / Needs Review). Give me a summary count of how many rows fall into each status category, plus a list of the flagged high-risk rows with a one-line reason for each. Do not submit or finalize any answers — this draft is input for a separate review and submission step.

You are helping me prepare the security-review package for the risky answers in our security questionnaire draft, ahead of sign-off by our security lead. Please ask me for: (1) the location of the draft questionnaire (spreadsheet or doc link), (2) the internal knowledge base/policy repository location, and (3) the customer name/deal this questionnaire is for, if I haven't already given these.

Actions to take:

Open the draft questionnaire and identify every row already flagged (or that you assess) as 'risky' — meaning answers touching data handling, encryption, incident response, subprocessors, access control, compliance certifications, or any answer that overstates, understates, or diverges from documented policy.
2. For each risky row, pull the corresponding policy or prior-answer evidence from the knowledge base and place it side-by-side with the drafted answer.
3. Note any gaps, contradictions, or unverifiable claims — e.g., where the draft claims a control exists but no supporting policy document was found.
4. Compile a single review packet (spreadsheet or doc) with columns: Question, Draft Answer, Supporting Policy/Evidence, Confidence Level, Flag/Concern.
5. Draft a short cover summary listing the highest-risk items needing the security lead's judgment first.

Do not alter the substantive content of any risky answer, do not mark anything as approved, and do not submit or forward the questionnaire to the customer or portal. Judging whether these draft answers accurately represent our actual controls and approving them as contractual representations is a decision only our security lead can make — this remains a human step, and I will handle it separately as it must stop for human sign-off.

Report back with: the compiled review packet, the cover summary of top-risk items, and a list of any evidence gaps you found, so I can hand this directly to our security lead for review.

If the portal itself requires a secondary human action beyond form submission (e.g., a phone verification step, contract e-signature, or manual customer approval), note that this remains a human step and stop there rather than attempting it.

You are helping me close out a completed security questionnaire by filing the final, reviewed answers back into our knowledge base so future questionnaires can reuse them. 4. Note the customer name and date of this questionnaire in each updated/new entry for traceability, without exposing confidential customer details beyond what's needed for internal reference.
5. Compile a short summary listing: how many answers were added, how many were updated, and any answers that were marked risky or reviewed by security, so I can spot-check accuracy.

Done looks like: every finalized answer is filed or updated in the knowledge base with proper tagging and linked evidence, and I have a clear summary report. Report back with the summary, links to the updated knowledge base sections, and flag anything ambiguous or unresolved for my review.

You are helping me check domain availability across multiple TLDs for my startup name using our chosen registrar, {{vendor}}.

You are helping me check whether my desired brand/company name is available as a matching handle across major social and developer platforms, so I can confirm consistent branding alongside my domain search.

Compile results into a simple table: rows = name variants, columns = platforms, cells = 'Available', 'Taken', or 'Unclear' (if the check was ambiguous or blocked, e.g., by a login wall). Note any platform where you could not get a reliable read.

You are helping me shortlist domain name candidates for my startup, including pricing and renewal costs. Compile the results into a clear table or list sorted by relevance (e.g., .com first, then other TLDs), showing name, TLD, availability, first-year price, renewal price, and source registrar. Highlight any renewal costs that seem unusually high relative to registration price.

Done looks like: a shortlist covering every candidate name across the requested TLDs, each with availability and both first-year and renewal pricing clearly documented, ready for me to review and pick a final domain. Report back the full table plus a short summary noting the best value options and any red flags on renewal pricing.

You are helping me register and pay for a domain through {{vendor}}, our chosen domain registrar. Because this action is asynchronous, after submission poll {{vendor}}'s domain status/lookup API (or dashboard) periodically to verify the registration has completed and is active — this confirmation may take time and remains a human step to finally verify receipt if {{vendor}} sends email confirmation outside the API.

You are helping me complete the DNS/SSL provisioning step for a domain I just purchased and registered at Name.com, with payment already processed via Stripe. Please act as an async step: kick off the work, then poll/verify until it's confirmed complete, since results may not be instant.

5. Poll {{vendor}}'s status (DNS propagation, SSL certificate issuance) until both DNS resolution and SSL are confirmed active — do not report success prematurely.

Done looks like: DNS records are live, SSL certificate is issued and auto-renewing, and the domain correctly resolves to the intended target over HTTPS.

Report back with: the DNS records created (type, name, value), SSL/certificate status, any custom domain/routing configuration applied, and confirmation timestamps from your verification polling. Flag any records or settings you could not create automatically so I can review them.

You are helping me prepare for vendor invoice payment by pulling all currently outstanding bills from our accounting system, {{vendor}}.

Done looks like: you have a complete, deduplicated list of all outstanding vendor bills with the fields above, a summary total of amounts owed, and a short note on any exceptions or bills requiring attention before payment.

Report back with: the total number of outstanding bills, total amount outstanding (by currency if applicable), the structured list/table of bills, and any flags or exceptions you found. You are helping me complete step fin_001:n2 of our 'Pay vendor invoices' process: checking our account balance before paying outstanding vendor invoices via wire transfer.

Done looks like: a clear summary table or list of account balances with a plain yes/no verdict on whether we have sufficient funds to proceed with the wire payments, plus any anomalies flagged. Do not initiate, schedule, or approve any wire transfers or payments as part of this step — this step is purely a balance check to inform the next step in the process. Just report the balance findings back to me.

You are helping me create a payment run in {{vendor}} (our startup banking platform) for all currently approved vendor bills, ready for wire transfer, but WITHOUT sending any money — a human must explicitly approve before payments go out.

5. Produce a clear payment run summary: total number of bills, total amount per currency, vendor names, and any flagged exceptions.

Done looks like: a fully prepared payment run in {{vendor}} (or a structured draft if API access to create it isn't available) listing every approved bill, amounts, destinations, and exceptions — with no transfer, batch transfer, or wire actually initiated or sent.

Report back to me with: the payment run summary, links or IDs to the draft run in {{vendor}} if created, the list of flagged/excluded bills with reasons, and then stop for human sign-off — do not approve, submit, or initiate the wire transfer yourself.

You are helping me post a payment summary for today's vendor invoice run to our team's chat channel in {{vendor}}.

You are helping me complete the 'Pull the bank transactions' step of our monthly bookkeeping close. We use {{vendor}} as our startup banking/spend platform. You are helping me complete the transaction categorization step of my monthly bookkeeping close using {{vendor}}, our accounting platform.

Report back with: the count of transactions categorized, the count flagged for review with reasons, and a list of any draft journal entries awaiting accountant sign-off. Do not post journal entries yourself or make final judgment calls on ambiguous items — leave those for human sign-off.

You are helping me close the books for the month by reconciling our bank statement in {{vendor}} before I give final sign-off. Please use my configured credentials to connect to {{vendor}} — if you need my company/organization identifier, the bank account name, or the statement period (start and end dates), ask me for these first.

Actions to take:

5. Prepare a checklist confirming: report received, cap table reconciled, no unresolved discrepancies, and memo/resolution ready for signature.

Do not accept, adopt, sign, or approve the valuation yourself, and do not instruct me to do so via automated action — this decision carries legal weight for IRS safe-harbor reliance and must be an officer's own authoritative act. When your review and drafts are complete, present the summary memo, checklist, and any flagged issues, and then stop for human sign-off.

You are helping me verify that our 409A valuation is current before we issue new stock options to team members. Please do the following:

4. If the valuation is stale or about to expire, check whether {{vendor}} supports ordering a new audit-ready 409A valuation in-platform generated from our live cap table, and prepare a summary of what that would involve (data it will use, estimated turnaround) — but do not initiate a purchase or submit any order; that remains a human step.
5. Cross-check the valuation's underlying cap table snapshot against our current cap table (stakeholders, share classes, vesting states) via {{vendor}}'s API to confirm no major discrepancies exist that would call the valuation into question.

When done, report back to me with: (a) whether the 409A is currently valid, (b) the valuation amount and expiration date, (c) any discrepancies found in the underlying cap table, and (d) if a refresh is needed, a prepared summary/checklist for ordering a new valuation so I can review and stop for human sign-off before proceeding with any purchase or grant.

You are helping me draft a Board Consent (Unanimous Written Consent in Lieu of Meeting) approving new stock option grants, as part of our stock option issuance process. This is a document-preparation task only — no filing or execution.

First, ask me for any missing details: (1) legal company name and state of incorporation, (2) current equity incentive plan name and adoption date (e.g., '2021 Equity Incentive Plan'), (3) list of grantees with title/role, number of shares/options per grantee, exercise (strike) price per share, vesting schedule (e.g., 4-year with 1-year cliff), and grant date, (4) names of all current board members and the date the consent will circulate, (5) whether a 409A valuation is current and its effective date, and (6) whether option agreements will be countersigned in Carta or another cap table system.

Also prepare a short checklist listing: the draft consent, the grantee/grant details table, and next steps (circulate to board, collect signatures, then record grants and issue option agreements once approved).

Do not send, distribute, or submit this consent to the board, and do not mark any grant as approved — stop for human sign-off. Report back with the drafted consent text, the grant summary table, and the checklist for my review.

You are helping me generate a stock option agreement for a new grant using {{vendor}}, our equity-management platform. You are helping me model how our outstanding SAFEs (and any convertible notes) convert into preferred stock as part of closing our priced equity round. Flag any SAFE or side letter terms that are ambiguous, inconsistent, or missing data needed to model conversion (e.g., unclear cap definitions, MFN clauses, conflicting pro-rata language).

Do not finalize or execute the conversion on the platform — this scenario is for review only. Flag any ambiguous or conflicting terms (e.g., unclear cap definitions, stacked discounts, side-letter overrides) that counsel should specifically weigh in on.

Once the memo and spreadsheet are ready, stop for human sign-off — do not send the package to counsel or authorize any conversion yourself. Report back with: the draft memo, the conversion spreadsheet, a list of flagged ambiguities, and a note that counsel's written confirmation is pending and must be tracked/polled for before execution proceeds.

You are helping me authorize credentials for a third-party vendor or custom MCP server so it can be connected to our system. Report back with: the vendor/service name, auth method, prepared checklist, any pre-filled fields, and the exact screen/step where I need to log in and approve. You are helping me connect a custom MCP server to my agent runtime so my agents can call its tools. The vendor for this MCP-infrastructure connection is {{vendor}} — do not substitute any other name.

You are helping me finish connecting a vendor or custom MCP server integration by running a smoke-test tool call and saving the connection. Report back with: the vendor/server name, the tool call you invoked, a summary of the response (success or failure with diagnosis), and confirmation that the connection was saved as verified.

You are helping me define requirements and constraints for selecting an AI assistant ({{vendor}}) to support knowledge-work tasks like document/presentation creation and organizing project context. This is step one of a vendor selection process (requirements → shortlist → comparison → trial → security review → negotiation), so your output here will feed later research and evaluation steps.

Using my answers, produce a structured requirements document covering:

- Non-functional requirements: security/compliance constraints, integration needs with my existing stack, performance/reliability expectations.
- Constraints: budget ceiling, seat count, deployment timeline, any vendors or approaches to exclude.
- Success criteria: how I'll know a candidate meets my needs (e.g., can produce an exportable deck from a prompt, can maintain context across a multi-file project).

Format the output as a clear markdown document with labeled sections (Functional Requirements, Non-Functional Requirements, Constraints, Success Criteria) so it can be handed directly to the next step (market research and shortlisting). Do not research or name specific products yet — this step is requirements-only. Report back with the completed requirements document and a short list of any open questions I still need to answer before shortlisting can begin.

You are helping me research and shortlist vendors in the "ai-assistants" market (products like {{vendor}}) as candidates for a function we need to support. Report back with the shortlist table, your top recommendations, and any open questions you need me to answer before we move to detailed comparison and trials.

You are helping me compare shortlisted software candidates for a specific function against my existing stack, using judged evidence, and produce a ranked recommendation. Explicitly check compatibility with each item in my current stack (data formats, APIs, auth methods, hosting model, language/framework support, etc.) and flag any gaps, extra middleware needed, or migration effort. Note evidence quality (official docs vs. marketing claims vs. third-party review) for each finding so I can judge reliability.

Produce a comparison table scoring each candidate against every requirement and stack-compatibility check, with a short evidence citation or note per score. Follow with a ranked list (best fit to worst) and a one-paragraph rationale per candidate explaining strengths, weaknesses, and stack-fit risks.

Done looks like: a clear ranked table plus written rationale for every shortlisted candidate, all major claims backed by cited sources, and explicit flags on any stack-compatibility risks or unknowns still needing verification.

Report back with the full comparison table, the ranking, the rationale summaries, and a list of any open questions or evidence gaps I should resolve before moving to trials.

You are helping me run hands-on agentic trials of the top candidate software options I've shortlisted for a specific function in my stack. After trials, produce a structured comparison document scoring each candidate against the requirements, with concrete evidence (not opinions) supporting each score, plus a short list of open questions or risks to raise before security review and negotiation.

Done looks like: each candidate has been actually exercised end-to-end (not just read about), a comparison scorecard exists with evidence-backed ratings, and a clear leader (or tie) emerges with rationale.

Report back with: the comparison scorecard, key findings per candidate, any blockers or unresolved risks, and your recommended next candidate(s) to carry into security review.

You are helping me complete a security and data review for a software vendor I'm considering onboarding. 6. Produce a single structured summary document with sections: Data Handling, Certifications & Gaps, Breach History, DPA Concerns, and an overall risk flag (low/medium/high) with reasoning.

Do not make any acceptance, approval, or onboarding decision yourself. This requires judgment from someone with security authority, so once your summary is ready, stop for human sign-off. Report back with the summary document and a short list of open questions or risks that need explicit human judgment before proceeding.
